aber.etymology: Recorded in Old and Middle High German as aber / aver, originally meaning 'again, further, afterwards' (preserved in abermals 'once again') before settling into the contrasting conjunction 'but, however'.

abgemacht.etymology: Lexicalized past participle of separable abmachen ('to settle an agreement'), used elliptically for es ist abgemacht ('it is settled'); see DWDS/Pfeifer under abmachen.

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): abmachen
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): abmachen

abhalten.etymology: Separable compound of ab- ('off, away', OHG aba) + strong verb halten ('to hold, keep', OHG haltan); documented in DWDS/Pfeifer under abhalten.

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): abhalten
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): abhalten

acht.etymology: Old and Middle High German ahto / aht continue the Indo-European numeral for 'eight', matching English 'eight' and Latin octō.

akkord.etymology: Pfeifer (DWDS) and Kluge trace Akkord to French accord ('harmony, agreement'), ultimately from Vulgar Latin *accordāre ('to bring hearts/strings into tune', ad + cor 'heart' / chorda 'string').

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Akkord
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Akkord

alt.etymology: Old and Middle High German alt originated as a past participle meaning 'grown up, nourished' (related to Latin alere 'to nourish'), identical in origin to English 'old'.

ander.etymology: Continues Old High German andar and Middle High German ander ('second, other'), formed with a comparative suffix from an Indo-European stem meaning 'the other of two', cognate with English 'other'.

anrufen.etymology: Separable compound of an ('at, to') + rufen ('to call, shout'). Originally 'to call out to someone', in the telephone age it became the standard verb for calling by phone.
anrufen.notes: Takes a direct accusative object in German (ich rufe meinen Bruder an).

anschauen.etymology: Separable compound of an ('at') + schauen ('to look, gaze', OHG scouwōn, cognate with English 'show'), meaning 'to look at, inspect'.

cognates.meaning: from the causative sense 'cause to look'

auf.etymology: Old and Middle High German ūf ('up, upon') underwent both the High German shift of *-p to -f and Early New High German diphthongization of ū to au.
auf.notes: Serves as preposition ('on'), separable verb prefix ('open / up'), and predicative adverb ('open').

aufmachen.etymology: Transparent separable compound of stressed prefix auf ('up, open') + machen ('make'), literally 'to make open'. In main clauses, machen sits in second position while auf closes the clause.

aufwachen.etymology: Separable compound of auf ('up') + wachen ('to be awake', OHG wahhēn), matching English 'wake up' piece for piece.
aufwachen.notes: Forms its perfect tense with sein (ist aufgewacht) because waking is a change of state.

aus.etymology: Continues Old and Middle High German ūz ('out, out of, from'), where long ū diphthongized regularly to au while High German shifted *-t to -z/-s.

bei.etymology: Continues Old and Middle High German bī ('near, beside, at'), diphthongized in Early New High German from long ī to ei.
bei.notes: Always governs the dative case; contracts with dem to beim.

bett.etymology: Old High German betti and Middle High German bette ('sleeping place, garden bed'), cognate with English 'bed'.

bitte.etymology: Shortened in 19th-century spoken German from ich bitte ('I ask, request', OHG bitten), mirroring how danke shortened from ich danke.

blau.etymology: Old and Middle High German blā (inflected blāwer) originally meant 'shimmering, lustrous, blue', also borrowed into Romance languages and thence into English 'blue'.

cognates.meaning: via Old French bleu from Germanic

bleiben.etymology: Continues Old High German bilīban and Middle High German belīben > blīben, where unstressed bi- syncopated to b- before l ('to remain, stay behind').

bogen.etymology: Old High German bogo and Middle High German boge ('bow, arch, curve'), formed from biegen ('to bend').

bogenfenster.etymology: Compound of Bogen ('arch, curve, bow', OHG bogo, from biegen 'to bend') + Fenster ('window', OHG venstar from Latin fenestra); see DWDS/Pfeifer under Bogenfenster.

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Bogenfenster
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Bogenfenster

brett.etymology: Pfeifer (DWDS) and Kluge trace Brett to OHG and MHG bret ('sawn plank, board'), an ablaut relative of Bord and cognate with Old English bred ('board, tablet').

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Brett
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Brett

brille.etymology: Late Middle High German berille ('reading lens, spectacles') came from der Beryll ('beryl crystal'), because early medieval magnifying lenses were ground from clear beryl.
brille.notes: Singular die Brille refers to one pair of glasses.

buch.etymology: Old and Middle High German buoh ('writing tablet, book') is closely linked to die Buche ('beech tree'), recalling early Germanic runes carved onto beechwood tablets.

bäckerin.etymology: Derived with the feminine agent suffix -in (OHG -inna) from Bäcker ('baker', OHG beckāri, from backen 'to bake'); see DWDS/Pfeifer under Bäckerin.

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Bäckerin
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Bäckerin

bücherregal.etymology: Compound of plural Bücher ('books', OHG buoh) and Regal ('shelving unit', borrowed in Early New High German from Italian regale / Latin rēgula 'straight lath, rule'); see DWDS/Pfeifer under Bücherregal and Regal.

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Bücherregal
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Bücherregal

cafémöbel.etymology: Compound of Café and Möbel ('piece of furniture', 17th c. from French meuble < Latin mōbilis 'movable'); see DWDS/Pfeifer under Café and Möbel.

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Möbel
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Möbel

cafétisch.etymology: Compound of Café (borrowed from French café, 'coffeehouse') and Tisch ('table', OHG tisc from Latin discus); see DWDS/Pfeifer under Café and Tisch.

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Tisch
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Tisch

d.etymology: Letter and solmization/pitch name continuing the Latin fourth letter D (pronounced [deː] in German), established in medieval gamut notation for the tone above C; see DWDS under D.

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): D
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): D

dafür.etymology: Pronominal adverb combining da(r)- ('there/that') + für ('for'), MHG dārvür; documented in DWDS/Pfeifer under dafür.

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): dafür
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): dafür

darum.etymology: Pronominal compound of da(r) ('there, that', OHG dār) + um ('around, concerning', OHG umbi), already OHG dārumbi ('around that, for that reason'); see DWDS/Pfeifer under darum.

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): darum
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): darum

dauern.etymology: Borrowed in Middle High German (tūren / dūren) via Old French durer from Latin dūrāre ('to harden, hold out, last'), sharing its Latin root with English 'endure' and 'duration'.

deckel.etymology: Pfeifer (DWDS) and Kluge derive Deckel (MHG deckel) with the Germanic instrument suffix -el from decken ('to cover, roof', OHG decken).

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Deckel
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Deckel

deckenlampe.etymology: Compound of Decke ('ceiling, cover', OHG deckī) and Lampe ('lamp'); documented in DWDS/Pfeifer under Deckenlampe.

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Deckenlampe
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Deckenlampe

dein.etymology: Continues Old and Middle High German dīn, the possessive counterpart of du, regularly diphthongized from long ī to ei in Early New High German.

denkmalamt.etymology: Compound of Denkmal ('historic monument') and Amt ('public office, authority', OHG ambaht, ultimately of Celtic origin); see DWDS/Pfeifer under Denkmal and Amt.

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Amt
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Amt

denkmalschutz.etymology: Recorded in DWDS/Pfeifer as Denkmal ('monument, memorial', coined by Luther from denken + Mal 'mark') + Schutz ('protection', from schützen).

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Denkmalschutz
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Denkmalschutz

der.etymology: The definite article developed from a West Germanic demonstrative meaning 'that', recorded in Old and Middle High German as der (masculine), diu (feminine), and daz (neuter). Over time unstressed pointing words became the everyday definite article while stressed uses remained demonstrative and relative pronouns.
der.notes: Modern der, die, das, den, dem, and des belong to one paradigm marking gender, number, and case.

dose.etymology: Pfeifer (DWDS) and Kluge trace Dose (17th c., via Low German/Dutch doos) to Late Latin / Greek dósis ('measured portion of medicine', later the small box holding it).

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Dose
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Dose

du.etymology: Continues Old and Middle High German dū / du, the inherited singular second-person pronoun across Indo-European languages. It remains the standard pronoun among family, close friends, children, and peers.

durch.etymology: Descends from Old High German duruh / durh and Middle High German durch ('through, across'), always governing the accusative case.

cognates.meaning: from one side to the other

duschwasser.etymology: Determinative compound of duschen / die Dusche ('shower', from French douche and Italian doccia 'water pipe') + das Wasser ('water').

dürfen.etymology: Continues Old High German durfan and Middle High German dürfen, originally meaning 'to need, require' (preserved in bedürfen) before developing into the modal of permission ('may, be allowed to').

ein.etymology: German ein continues Old and Middle High German ein, originally the cardinal numeral 'one'. Just as English 'a/an' grew out of 'one', unstressed ein became the indefinite article while stressed ein kept its numerical sense.
ein.notes: Indefinite ein has no plural; plural indefinite nouns appear without an article.

empfang.etymology: Back-formation from empfangen ('to receive, welcome', OHG intfāhan), naming both the act of welcoming someone and a hotel or guesthouse reception desk.

erdgeschoss.etymology: Pfeifer (DWDS) and Kluge explain Erdgeschoss (18th c.) as Erde ('earth, ground') + Geschoss ('storey of a building', originally a 'shooting up' or 'projection' of masonry, from schießen).

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Erdgeschoss
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Erdgeschoss

erinnern.etymology: Pfeifer (DWDS) and Kluge explain erinnern (16th c., built on inner 'inner, internal') as originally meaning 'to make someone inwardly aware of something', whence reflexive sich erinnern 'to recall'.

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): erinnern
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): erinnern

ersatzsicherung.etymology: Compound of Ersatz ('replacement, spare', from ersetzen 'to replace') + Sicherung ('electrical fuse', from sicher < Latin sēcūrus); see DWDS/Pfeifer under Ersatz and Sicherung.

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Sicherung
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Sicherung

erste.etymology: Continues Middle High German ēr(e)st and Old High German ērist, the historical superlative of ē ('earlier, before', modern eher), meaning 'earliest, first'.

es.etymology: Descends from Old High German iz and Middle High German ez, the neuter third-person singular pronoun. Besides referring back to neuter nouns like das Zimmer, it serves as the grammatical subject in expressions like es regnet and es gibt.

fenstergriff.etymology: Compound of Fenster ('window', OHG venstar) and Griff ('handle, grip', OHG grif, verbal abstract of greifen 'to grasp'); see DWDS/Pfeifer under Fenstergriff.

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Fenstergriff
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Fenstergriff

finden.etymology: Old High German findan became Middle High German vinden, originally 'to come upon while walking' before settling into 'to find, discover'.

flur.etymology: Pfeifer (DWDS) and Kluge connect MHG vluor ('flat ground, paved entrance') directly with English floor; in modern German masculine der Flur specialized into 'corridor, entrance hall'.

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Flur
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Flur

flurwand.etymology: Compound of Flur ('hallway, corridor') and Wand ('interior wall', OHG want); see DWDS/Pfeifer under Flur and Wand.

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Wand
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Wand

foto.etymology: Pfeifer (DWDS) and Kluge record Foto (late 19th c., neuter after das Bild) as a clipping of Fotografie, coined from Greek phōs / phōtós ('light') + gráphein ('to write, draw').

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Foto
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Foto

freihalten.etymology: Separable compound of adjective frei ('free, unoccupied', OHG frī) + halten ('to hold, keep'); documented in DWDS/Pfeifer under freihalten.

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): freihalten
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): freihalten

freitagsplan.etymology: Compound of Freitag ('Friday', OHG frīatag) with linking -s- and Plan ('plan', 18th c. from French plan); see DWDS/Pfeifer under Freitag and Plan.

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Plan
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Plan

freund.etymology: Old High German friunt and Middle High German vriunt originated as an ancient present participle meaning 'loving one', cognate with English 'friend'.

früh.etymology: Old High German fruo and Middle High German vruo / früeje ('early, in the morning'), sharing an Indo-European prefix root with vor ('before').

frühstück.etymology: Middle High German vrüestücke joined früe ('early') with stücke ('piece, morsel of bread'), originally naming the early piece of bread eaten at daybreak before becoming the general word for 'breakfast'.

gast.etymology: Old and Middle High German gast ('stranger, visitor, guest') shares its Indo-European root *ghos-ti- with both English 'guest' and Latin hostis / hospes ('host, hospitality').

geben.etymology: Continues Old High German geban and Middle High German geben ('to give, hand over'). Since Early New High German the impersonal phrase es gibt ('it gives') has served as the standard expression for 'there is / there are'.
geben.notes: In es gibt, the noun phrase that follows stands in the accusative case (es gibt heißen Tee).

geheim.etymology: Pfeifer (DWDS) and Kluge derive geheim (MHG geheim 'belonging to the home, intimate, confidential') from Heim ('home'), shifting from 'familiar within the household' to 'kept private, secret'.

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): geheim
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): geheim

geheimnis.etymology: Formed in Early New High German with the abstract noun suffix -nis from geheim ('belonging to the home, trusted, secret', containing Heim 'home').

gehen.etymology: Continues Old and Middle High German gēn / gān ('to walk, go'), paired historically in its past forms ging and gegangen with the fuller stem gangan.

geld.etymology: Old and Middle High German gelt meant 'payment, tribute, recompense', derived from gelten ('to be worth, repay') before becoming the everyday word for 'money'.

gespräch.etymology: Pfeifer (DWDS) and Kluge explain Gespräch (OHG gisprāhhi, MHG gespræche) as a collective Ge- noun from sprechen ('to speak'), naming reciprocal speech between people.

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Gespräch
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Gespräch

glasdach.etymology: Compound of Glas ('glass', OHG glas) + Dach ('roof', OHG dah, cognate with English thatch); documented in DWDS/Pfeifer under Glasdach.

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Glasdach
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Glasdach

glaslampe.etymology: Compound of Glas ('glass', OHG glas) and Lampe ('lamp'); see DWDS/Pfeifer under Glas and Lampe.

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Lampe
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Lampe

glänzend.etymology: Participial adjective of glänzen ('to shine, gleam', MHG glenzen, from Glanz 'lustre, brightness'); documented in DWDS/Pfeifer under glänzend.

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): glänzend
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): glänzend

gut.etymology: Old and Middle High German guot originally meant 'fitting neatly together' (from the same root as gather and Gitter) before generalizing to 'good, well'.

haben.etymology: Recorded as Old High German habēn and Middle High German haben ('to hold, possess'). Shortened spoken stems in Middle High German (hān, hāst, hāt) explain why modern du hast and er hat drop the -b-.

halb.etymology: Old and Middle High German halb ('half; side'). In German clock time, halb acht looks ahead toward the coming hour ('halfway to eight' = 7:30).

hauptsicherung.etymology: Compound of intensifying prefixoid Haupt- ('chief, main', originally 'head', OHG houbit) + Sicherung ('fuse, safeguard', from sichern 'to make safe'); see DWDS/Pfeifer under Hauptsicherung.

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Hauptsicherung
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Hauptsicherung

haus.etymology: Old and Middle High German hūs ('dwelling, house') diphthongized its long ū to au in Early New High German, matching English 'house' from the same Germanic noun.
haus.notes: Preserves the old dative singular ending -e in the fixed expression zu Hause ('at home').

heiß.etymology: Old and Middle High German heiz ('hot, burning') shifted Germanic *-t to -z/-ß, matching English 'hot' from the same root as Hitze ('heat').

heißen.etymology: Continues Old High German heizan and Middle High German heizen ('to command, call, be named'), preserving an ancient Germanic passive trace in the sense 'to be called' (wie heißen Sie?).

heute.etymology: Old High German hiutu (Middle High German hiute) contracted an old instrumental phrase *hiu tagu meaning 'on this day', disguising an ancient compound inside a two-syllable word.

hier.etymology: Recorded as Old High German hiar and Middle High German hie(r), formed from the Germanic proximal demonstrative stem *hi- ('this') + a locative -r suffix.

hintere.etymology: Pfeifer (DWDS) and Kluge trace attributive hintere (OHG hintaro, MHG hindere) as an old comparative-like spatial adjective built on hinter ('behind', cognate with English hinder).

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): hintere
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): hintere

hochheben.etymology: Separable compound of hoch ('up, high', OHG hōh) + strong verb heben ('to lift, heave', OHG heffen, cognate with English heave); see DWDS/Pfeifer under hochheben.

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): hochheben
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): hochheben

hof.etymology: Continues Old and Middle High German hof ('enclosed yard, farmstead, princely court'). From 'royal court' also came the adjective höflich ('courteous, polite').

hofbaum.etymology: Compound of Hof ('courtyard', OHG hof) and Baum ('tree', OHG boum); see DWDS/Pfeifer under Hof and Baum.

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Baum
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Baum

hofdach.etymology: Compound of Hof ('courtyard', OHG hof) and Dach ('roof', OHG dah); see DWDS/Pfeifer under Hof and Dach.

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Dach
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Dach

holzdeckel.etymology: Compound of Holz ('wood', OHG holz) + Deckel ('lid, cover', MHG deckel, an instrument derivative of decken 'to cover'); documented via DWDS/Pfeifer under Deckel.

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Holzdeckel
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Holzdeckel

holzregal.etymology: Compound of Holz ('wood', OHG holz) and Regal ('shelf', from Latin rēgula 'wooden strip, rule'); see DWDS/Pfeifer under Holzregal.

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Holzregal
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Holzregal

holzzug.etymology: Transparent compound of das Holz ('wood', OHG holz) + der Zug ('train'), naming a carved wooden toy train.

ich.etymology: Inherited from West Germanic *ek via Old High German ih and Middle High German ich, where the High German consonant shift turned final *-k after a vowel into the fricative -ch.
ich.notes: Unlike English 'I', German ich is capitalized only at the start of a sentence.

ihr.etymology: Combines two historical threads: Old High German ir ('you all', plural of du) and ira / iro ('of her / of them'), which gave rise to the possessive determiner ihr ('her/their') and capitalized polite Ihr ('your').

history.meaning: ye (2nd pl.) / of her, of them

in.etymology: Inherited unchanged in spelling from Old and Middle High German in, governing the dative for static location ('in') and the accusative for motion into a space ('into').
in.notes: Contracts with dem to im and with das to ins.

ja.etymology: Recorded as jā in both Old and Middle High German across Germanic languages. Alongside its primary use as 'yes', unstressed mid-sentence ja functions as a modal particle appealing to shared knowledge.

jahrzehntelang.etymology: Compound of plural Jahrzehnte ('decades', Jahr + zehn) + durational suffixoid -lang ('for the length of'); documented in DWDS/Pfeifer under jahrzehntelang.

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): jahrzehntelang
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): jahrzehntelang

kaffee.etymology: Entered German around 1700 via French café and Italian caffè, ultimately from Ottoman Turkish kahve and Arabic qahwa. Masculine der Kaffee names the beverage, while neuter das Café names the coffeehouse.

kein.etymology: Recorded in Middle High German as kein, shortened from dehein ('any at all') under negative influence from nihein ('not one'). It fused negation directly with the indefinite article paradigm to negate nouns.
kein.notes: Takes the same endings as mein and ein in the singular, plus plural keine.

kennen.etymology: Middle High German kennen ('to know, recognize') goes back to West Germanic causative *kannjan ('to make known'), from the same root family as können.
kennen.notes: Used for familiarity with people, places, and things, whereas wissen is used for facts.

klatschen.etymology: Pfeifer (DWDS) and Kluge describe klatschen (16th c.) as an expressive onomatopoeic verb imitating the sharp slap of palms or splashing water.

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): klatschen
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): klatschen

klick.etymology: Pfeifer (DWDS) and Kluge describe Klick / klicken as a sound-imitative formation mimicking a short metallic snap, reinforced in modern German by English click.

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Klick
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Klick

knall.etymology: Pfeifer (DWDS) and Kluge derive Knall from MHG knal ('sharp crack, bang'), verbal abstract of knallen / MHG erknellen ('to resound, burst with a crack').

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Knall
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Knall

koffer.etymology: Borrowed via French coffre ('chest, trunk') from Latin cophinus and Greek kóphinos ('basket'). As travel shifted from wooden trunks to portable cases, Koffer became the standard word for 'suitcase'.

kommen.etymology: Descends from Old High German queman and Middle High German komen ('to come, arrive'), losing its initial labial element kw- before rounded vowels.

kuchen.etymology: Continues Old High German kuocho and Middle High German kuoche ('cake, baked pastry'), distantly related through West Germanic baking vocabulary to English 'cookie' (via Dutch koekje).

kupferdraht.etymology: Compound of Kupfer ('copper', OHG kupfar from Late Latin cuprum 'Cypriot metal') + Draht ('wire', OHG drāt); documented in DWDS/Pfeifer under Kupferdraht.

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Kupferdraht
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Kupferdraht

können.etymology: Descends from Old High German kunnan and Middle High German kunnen / künnen, a preterite-present verb that originally meant 'to know how to, understand mentally' before shifting to general ability ('can').
können.notes: Because preterite-presents were originally past forms, ich kann and er kann take no -e or -t ending.

küchenofen.etymology: Compound of Küche ('kitchen') + Ofen ('oven, stove', OHG ovan, exact cognate with English oven); documented in DWDS/Pfeifer under Küchenofen.

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Küchenofen
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Küchenofen

küchenwand.etymology: Compound of Küche ('kitchen', OHG kuhhīna from Vulgar Latin coquīna) with linking -n- + Wand ('wall', OHG want, originally a woven wattle wall, from winden 'to wind'); see DWDS/Pfeifer under Küchenwand.

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Küchenwand
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Küchenwand

kühlschrank.etymology: 20th-century transparent household compound joining kühl ('cool', OHG kuoli) with der Schrank ('cupboard, cabinet'), literally 'cool-cupboard'.
kühlschrank.notes: Masculine der Kühlschrank takes its gender from der Schrank.

lehrerin.etymology: Feminine derivative in -in from Lehrer ('teacher', MHG lērære, agent noun of lehren 'to teach', cognate with English lore); see DWDS/Pfeifer under Lehrerin.

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Lehrerin
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Lehrerin

leicht.etymology: Pfeifer (DWDS) and Kluge trace leicht through OHG līht(i) and MHG līht ('not heavy, effortless'), exact Germanic cognate with English light ('not heavy').

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): leicht
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): leicht

leinentuch.etymology: Compound of Leinen ('linen fabric', OHG līnīn, from Lein / Latin līnum 'flax') and Tuch ('cloth', OHG tuoh); documented in DWDS/Pfeifer under Leinentuch.

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Leinentuch
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Leinentuch

leise.etymology: Pfeifer (DWDS) and Kluge trace leise to OHG līso and MHG līse ('gently, softly, slowly'), shifting from gentle movement to soft sound.

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): leise
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): leise

lesecafé.etymology: Modern compound of verb stem lese- (from lesen 'to read', OHG lesan 'to gather, read') + Café (French café); see DWDS/Pfeifer under lesen and Café.

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Café
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Café

lesen.etymology: Old High German lesan and Middle High German lesen originally meant 'to gather, pick up' (still used in Weinlese 'grape harvest'), transferred like Latin legere to gathering letters into words ('to read').

leuchten.etymology: Pfeifer (DWDS) and Kluge derive leuchten (OHG liuhten, MHG liuhten) directly from Licht ('light', OHG lioht), matching English light (up).

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): leuchten
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): leuchten

lied.etymology: Pfeifer (DWDS) and Kluge trace Lied through OHG liod and MHG liet ('stanza, song') to a common Germanic poetic term (compare Old English lēoþ 'song, poem').

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Lied
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Lied

linke.etymology: Pfeifer (DWDS) and Kluge trace link / linke to OHG lenka ('left hand') and MHG linc ('awkward, left-handed'), from which adverbial links developed with genitive -s.

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): link
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): link

liste.etymology: Pfeifer (DWDS) and Kluge trace Liste (late 16th c.) to Italian lista ('narrow strip of paper, register'), itself an early Germanic loan into Romance (compare OHG līsta 'border, strip').

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Liste
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Liste

luft.etymology: Pfeifer (DWDS) and Kluge trace Luft to OHG and MHG luft ('air, sky, breeze'), a distinctive Germanic word (compare Old English lyft 'air, sky' and English loft).

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Luft
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Luft

machen.etymology: Old High German mahhōn and Middle High German machen originally meant 'to knead, join, construct' (originally building clay walls) before broadening into the everyday verb 'to make, do'.

mai.etymology: Pfeifer (DWDS) and Kluge derive Mai (OHG meio, MHG meie) from Latin (mēnsis) Māius, named after the Italic fertility goddess Maia.

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Mai
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Mai

maßband.etymology: Compound of Maß ('measure', MHG māz, from messen 'to measure') and Band ('ribbon, strip', OHG bant, from binden); documented in DWDS/Pfeifer under Maßband.

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Maßband
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Maßband

mein.etymology: Goes back to Old and Middle High German mīn, formed from the first-person stem seen in mich and mir. Diphthongization of long ī produced modern mein.

messingschalter.etymology: Compound of Messing ('brass') and Schalter ('switch', agent/instrument noun from schalten 'to switch, direct'); see DWDS/Pfeifer under Messing and Schalter.

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Schalter
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Schalter

messingschloss.etymology: Transparent determinative compound of Messing ('brass', MHG messinc) and Schloss ('lock', MHG sloz, from schließen 'to lock'); see Pfeifer/DWDS and Kluge under Messing and Schloss.

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Schloss
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Schloss

messingschlüssel.etymology: Determinative compound of Messing ('brass') + der Schlüssel ('key'). As in all German compound nouns, the final element der Schlüssel sets the masculine gender and declension.

mit.etymology: Descends from Old High German mit(i) and Middle High German mit ('among, together with'), sharing a root with Mitte ('middle'). It always governs the dative case.

mitnehmen.etymology: Separable compound of mit ('along, with') + nehmen ('to take', OHG neman), expressing taking an item or person along on one's way.

mittagessen.etymology: Compound of Mittag ('midday', OHG mittitag) and nominalized infinitive Essen ('meal, eating', OHG ezzan); documented in DWDS/Pfeifer under Mittagessen.

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Mittagessen
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Mittagessen

monatsende.etymology: Compound of Monat ('month', OHG mānōd, related to Mond 'moon') + Ende ('end', OHG enti); documented in DWDS/Pfeifer under Monatsende.

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Monatsende
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Monatsende

morgen.etymology: Old High German morgan and Middle High German morgen meant 'morning, dawn'. Phrases like morgen früh ('in the morning') shifted to refer to the next morning, giving lowercase morgen the adverbial sense 'tomorrow'.
morgen.notes: Capitalized der Morgen means 'morning'; lowercase morgen means 'tomorrow'.

morgensonne.etymology: Compound of Morgen ('morning', OHG morgan) and Sonne ('sun', OHG sunna); documented in DWDS/Pfeifer under Morgensonne.

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Morgensonne
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Morgensonne

musik.etymology: Pfeifer (DWDS) and Kluge trace Musik (MHG mūsīke, re-accented in the 16th c. under French/Latin influence) to Latin mūsica and Greek mousikḗ (téchnē), 'art of the Muses'.

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Musik
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Musik

möbel.etymology: Pfeifer (DWDS) and Kluge derive Möbel (17th c.) from French meuble ('movable property, piece of furniture'), going back to Latin mōbilis ('movable', from movēre).

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Möbel
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Möbel

mögen.etymology: From Old High German magan / mugan and Middle High German mügen ('to have power, be able', related to Macht 'might'). Today indicative ich mag means 'I like', while subjunctive ich möchte / möchten Sie means 'would like'.

müssen.etymology: From Old High German muozan and Middle High German müezen, another preterite-present verb. In older German it meant 'to find room or opportunity, may', before narrowing to obligation ('must, have to').
müssen.notes: Negated nicht müssen means 'do not have to', whereas English 'must not' corresponds to nicht dürfen.

nach.etymology: Old High German nāh and Middle High German nāch originally meant 'near, close behind' (related to nah 'near' and Nachbar 'neighbour'), developing into 'toward' and temporal 'after'.

nachrechnen.etymology: Separable compound of nach- ('after, again for verification') + rechnen ('to calculate, reckon', OHG rehhanōn, cognate with English reckon); see DWDS/Pfeifer under nachrechnen.

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): nachrechnen
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): nachrechnen

nachsehen.etymology: Separable compound of nach- ('after, following up') + strong verb sehen ('to see, look', OHG sehan); documented in DWDS/Pfeifer under nachsehen.

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): nachsehen
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): nachsehen

nachttischlampe.etymology: Three-part compound of die Nacht ('night') + der Tisch ('table') + die Lampe ('lamp'), literally 'night-table-lamp' for a bedside reading lamp.

name.etymology: Continues Old High German namo and Middle High German name, an ancient Indo-European word for a personal or object designation.
name.notes: Follows weak-mixed declension: den Namen, dem Namen, des Namens.

nehmen.etymology: Continues Old High German neman and Middle High German nemen ('to take, grasp'), a core strong verb (nimmt, nahm, genommen).

cognates.meaning: relics of Old English niman ('to take')

nennen.etymology: Pfeifer (DWDS) and Kluge trace nennen (OHG nemnen, MHG nennen) to a Germanic derivative of Name ('name'), cognate with Old English nemnan ('to name').

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): nennen
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): nennen

nicht.etymology: Old High German niwiht combined the negative particle ni with wiht ('thing, creature'), literally 'not a thing'. Through Middle High German niht it weakened from an emphatic 'nothing' into the standard clause negator 'not'.

noch.etymology: Old High German noh and Middle High German noch combined nu ('now') with an enclitic particle meaning 'also, and', yielding 'even now, still, yet'.

nussbaum.etymology: Compound of Nuss ('nut, walnut', OHG nuz) and Baum ('tree, timber', OHG boum); Pfeifer (DWDS) notes its standard craft use for dark walnut wood.

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Nussbaum
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Nussbaum

onkel.etymology: Pfeifer (DWDS) and Kluge record Onkel as an 18th-century borrowing from French oncle, which descends from Latin avunculus ('maternal uncle', literally 'little grandfather', from avus).

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Onkel
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Onkel

peng.etymology: Recorded in DWDS/Pfeifer (19th c.) as an expressive sound-imitative interjection echoing a sharp bang or shot.

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): peng
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): peng

pension.etymology: Borrowed in the 18th century from French pension ('board and lodging payment, boarding house'), from Latin pēnsiō ('payment, weighing out'). In German it names a cosy, small guesthouse.

pfeil.etymology: Pfeifer (DWDS) and Kluge trace Pfeil through OHG pfīl and MHG pfīl as an early West Germanic borrowing from Latin pīlum ('heavy javelin'), showing the High German shift of p- to pf-.

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Pfeil
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Pfeil

rathaus.etymology: Middle High German rāthūs joined rāt ('town council, counsel') with hūs ('house'), naming the seat of municipal government on German market squares since the Middle Ages.

raus.etymology: Colloquial apheresis of directional adverb heraus ('out this way', her + aus); documented in DWDS/Pfeifer under raus.

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): raus
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): raus

regenfrühling.etymology: Compound of Regen ('rain', OHG regan) and Frühling ('spring', 15th-c. derivative of früh 'early', naming the early season of the year); see DWDS/Pfeifer under Regen and Frühling.

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Frühling
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Frühling

reifenpanne.etymology: Compound of der Reifen ('tyre, hoop') + die Panne ('mechanical breakdown, mishap', borrowed around 1900 from French panne in early aviation and motoring).

reinkommen.etymology: Everyday spoken shortening of hereinkommen: directional rein- ('in here') + kommen ('to come', OHG queman); documented in DWDS/Pfeifer under reinkommen.

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): reinkommen
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): reinkommen

reinpassen.etymology: Colloquial separable compound of shortened directional prefix rein- (from herein 'in here') + passen ('to fit', MHG passen from French passer); see DWDS/Pfeifer under reinpassen and passen.

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): reinpassen
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): reinpassen

reparatur.etymology: Pfeifer (DWDS) and Kluge derive Reparatur (16th/17th c.) from Late Latin reparātūra ('restoration'), built on Latin reparāre ('to make ready again, restore').

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Reparatur
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Reparatur

rückseite.etymology: Recorded in DWDS/Pfeifer (18th c.) as a compound of Rück- (from Rücken 'back', OHG rucki) and Seite ('side', OHG sīta).

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Rückseite
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Rückseite

rührei.etymology: Kitchen compound joining the stem of rühren ('to stir', OHG ruoren) with das Ei ('egg'), literally 'stir-egg' for scrambled eggs.

schalter.etymology: Pfeifer (DWDS) and Kluge trace Schalter (MHG schalter 'bolt, slider') to schalten ('to push, shift, switch', OHG skaltan 'to shove a boat with a pole'); the electrical sense arose in the late 19th century.

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Schalter
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Schalter

schieben.etymology: Pfeifer (DWDS) and Kluge trace schieben through OHG skioban and MHG schieben ('to push, thrust'), exact Germanic cognate with English shove.

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): schieben
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): schieben

schleifen.etymology: Pfeifer (DWDS) and Kluge trace strong schleifen (OHG slīfan, MHG slīfen 'to glide, whet, polish') to a Germanic root meaning 'to slip smoothly across a surface' (compare English slip).

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): schleifen
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): schleifen

schloss.etymology: Pfeifer (DWDS) and Kluge derive Schloss (OHG sloz, MHG sloz) from schließen ('to lock, shut', OHG sliozan); it meant first a bolt or lock and later a locked fortification or palace.

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Schloss
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Schloss

schlüssel.etymology: Old High German sluzzil and Middle High German slüzzel were formed with the instrument suffix *-ila from schließen (OHG sliozan 'to lock, bolt'), literally 'the locker / opener'.

schrank.etymology: Middle High German schranc originally meant 'wooden lattice, barrier, enclosed shelving' before becoming the standard German word for a tall cupboard or wardrobe.

schuh.etymology: Old High German scuoh and Middle High German schuoch ('shoe'), an inherited Germanic word for protective footwear.

schwarzweißfoto.etymology: Compound of copulative adjective schwarzweiß ('black-and-white') and Foto (clipping of Fotografie, Greek phōs 'light' + gráphein 'to draw'); see DWDS/Pfeifer under Schwarzweißfoto.

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Schwarzweißfoto
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Schwarzweißfoto

schwelle.etymology: Pfeifer (DWDS) and Kluge trace Schwelle through OHG swelli and MHG swelle ('foundation beam, sill'), exact cognate with English sill.

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Schwelle
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Schwelle

sein.etymology: Modern sein merges three ancient Indo-European roots: *bheu- ('grow, become') in bin and bist, *es- ('be') in ist and sind, and *wes- ('dwell, remain', OHG wesan) in war and gewesen. A separate homonymous stem OHG sīn produced the possessive sein ('his/its').

history.meaning: to be; to dwell or remain

servieren.etymology: Borrowed via French servir ('to serve at table') from Latin servīre, integrated with the standard German loan-verb suffix -ieren.
servieren.notes: Verbs ending in -ieren form their past participle without ge- (serviert).

setzen.etymology: Old High German sezzen and Middle High German setzen originated as the causative of sitzen ('to sit'), literally meaning 'to cause to sit, place'. Used reflexively (sich setzen), it means 'to sit down'.

sich.etymology: Continues Old High German sih and Middle High German sich, the inherited third-person reflexive pronoun; also used in modern German with polite Sie.

sie.etymology: Old High German siu / sī ('she') and sie ('they') converged in modern lowercase sie. In Early New High German, capitalized third-person plural Sie became the standard polite form of address for one or more adults.
sie.notes: Capitalization in writing (Sie, Ihnen, Ihr) distinguishes polite 'you' from 'she' or 'they'.

so.etymology: Continues Old and Middle High German sō ('in this manner, thus'), used both for manner ('like this') and degree ('so quiet').

sollen.etymology: From Old High German scolan / solan and Middle High German soln ('to owe, be obliged to'), related to Schuld ('debt, fault') and English 'shall / should'.

stapeln.etymology: Pfeifer (DWDS) and Kluge derive stapeln from Low German stapelen ('to pile in stacks'), built on Stapel ('wooden post, pile of goods', cognate with English staple).

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): stapeln
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): stapeln

staubig.etymology: Derived with adjective suffix -ig from Staub ('dust', OHG stoub, related to stieben 'to fly like sparks or dust'); see DWDS/Pfeifer under staubig.

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): staubig
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): staubig

steinboden.etymology: Compound of Stein ('stone', OHG stein) and Boden ('floor, bottom', OHG bodam, cognate with English bottom); see DWDS/Pfeifer under Steinboden.

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Steinboden
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Steinboden

stoffdraht.etymology: Compound of Stoff ('cloth, fabric', 17th c. via Dutch stof from Old French estoffe) and Draht ('wire', OHG drāt, literally 'twisted thread', from drehen); see DWDS/Pfeifer under Stoff and Draht.

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Draht
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Draht

straße.etymology: An early West Germanic borrowing (OHG strāza, MHG strāze) from Late Latin (via) strāta ('paved Roman road'), the same Latin phrase that gave English 'street'.

stuhl.etymology: Old and Middle High German stuol ('seat, throne, chair') derives from the root of stehen ('to stand'), originally naming an upright wooden seat with a backrest.

cognates.meaning: seat (narrowed in English to backless seat)

stumm.etymology: Pfeifer (DWDS) and Kluge trace stumm (OHG and MHG stum) to a Germanic root *stamma- / *stumma- meaning 'checked, halting in speech' (related to stammeln 'to stammer').

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): stumm
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): stumm

tag.etymology: Recorded as Old High German tag and Middle High German tac, inherited from Proto-Germanic *dagaz ('daylight hours, day').

taschenlampe.etymology: Compound of die Tasche ('pocket, bag') + linking -n- + die Lampe ('lamp'), literally 'pocket-lamp' for a handheld electric flashlight.

taste.etymology: Pfeifer (DWDS) and Kluge explain Taste (17th c., originally a keyboard key) as borrowed from Italian tasto ('touch, fret, key'), itself from tastare ('to touch, feel').

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Taste
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Taste

tee.etymology: Brought to Europe in the 17th century by Dutch maritime traders (Dutch thee) from Hokkien Chinese tê ('tea'), contrasting with Mandarin chá routes.

telefonnummer.etymology: Compound of das Telefon ('telephone', from Greek tēle 'far' + phōnē 'voice') and die Nummer ('number', from Italian numero / Latin numerus). Feminine die Nummer determines the gender.

testen.etymology: Pfeifer (DWDS) and Kluge record testen (20th c.) as borrowed from English to test, itself from Old French test / Latin testum ('earthenware assaying cupel used to test precious metals').

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): testen
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): testen

teuer.etymology: Pfeifer (DWDS) and Kluge trace teuer through OHG tiuri ('precious, valued, costly') and MHG tiure, exact cognate with English dear.

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): teuer
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): teuer

tisch.etymology: Old High German tisc and Middle High German tisch were borrowed early from Latin discus / Greek dískos ('round platter, quoit'); because medieval tabletops were lifted onto trestles like large platters, the word came to mean 'table'.

toast.etymology: Pfeifer (DWDS) and Kluge record Toast ('toasted bread') as a 19th/20th-century borrowing from English toast, which goes back via Old French toster to Latin torrēre / tostum ('to parch, scorch').

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Toast
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Toast

tschüss.etymology: Entered standard colloquial German via Low German adjüs / atschüs, adapted from Romance farewells (French adieu / Spanish adiós, from Latin ad Deum 'to God').

tür.etymology: Continues Old High German turi and Middle High German tür (originally dual/plural forms for double-leaf doors), cognate with English 'door' and related to neuter das Tor ('gate').

türschlüssel.etymology: Determinative compound of Tür ('door', OHG turi) and Schlüssel ('key', OHG sluzzil, from schließen 'to lock'), recorded in DWDS/Pfeifer under Türschlüssel.

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Türschlüssel
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Türschlüssel

um.etymology: From Old High German umbi and Middle High German umbe ('around, on both sides'). In modern German it marks spatial encirclement, exact clock hours (um zwölf Uhr), and purpose clauses with zu.

undicht.etymology: Transparent prefixation of negative un- + dicht ('tight, dense, waterproof', MHG dīhte); documented in DWDS/Pfeifer under undicht.

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): undicht
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): undicht

verdienen.etymology: Recorded as Old High German ferdionōn and Middle High German verdienen, combining unstressed inseparable ver- with dienen ('to serve', from dīhsmo / dio 'servant').
verdienen.notes: Because ver- is unstressed and inseparable, the past participle is verdient without ge-.

vermögen.etymology: Pfeifer (DWDS) and Kluge explain Vermögen (MHG vermügen) as the nominalized infinitive of vermögen ('to have power or means'), shifting from 'capability, power' to 'financial assets, fortune'.

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Vermögen
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Vermögen

von.etymology: From Old High German fona / fon and Middle High German von(e), marking origin, agency, or possession in place of the genitive; contracts with dem to vom.

wachen.etymology: Old High German wahhēn and Middle High German wachen ('to stay awake, keep watch'), sharing its Germanic root with die Wache ('guard, watch') and English 'wake / watch'.

wandlampe.etymology: Compound of Wand ('wall', OHG want) and Lampe ('lamp', MHG lampe from French lampe < Greek lampás 'torch'); see DWDS/Pfeifer under Wandlampe.

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Wandlampe
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Wandlampe

warm.etymology: Preserved unchanged in spelling through Old High German, Middle High German, and Modern German warm, naming pleasant, moderate heat.

wasser.etymology: Old High German wazzar and Middle High German wazzer continue the ancient Indo-European water root, with High German shifting Germanic *-t- between vowels to -zz-/-ss-.

wecken.etymology: Pfeifer (DWDS) and Kluge explain wecken (OHG wecken, MHG wecken) as the old Germanic causative of wachen ('to be awake'), literally 'to cause to be awake'.

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): wecken
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): wecken

wegräumen.etymology: Separable compound of directional adverb weg ('away', MHG enwec 'on the way') + räumen ('to clear, make space', OHG rūmen, from Raum 'space'); see DWDS/Pfeifer under wegräumen.

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): wegräumen
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): wegräumen

wind.etymology: Pfeifer (DWDS) and Kluge trace Wind (OHG and MHG wint) to an Indo-European participial formation meaning 'the blowing one' (compare Latin ventus and English wind).

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Wind
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Wind

wintergarten.etymology: Recorded in DWDS/Pfeifer from the late 18th century as a compound of Winter ('winter', OHG wintar) and Garten ('garden', OHG garto), naming a glazed conservatory heated or sheltered against frost.

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Wintergarten
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Wintergarten

winterteestube.etymology: Compound of Winter ('winter') + Tee ('tea') + Stube ('warm sitting room, parlour', OHG stuba, originally a heated room with a stove); see DWDS/Pfeifer under Teestube and Stube.

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Teestube
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Teestube

wir.etymology: Inherited from Old and Middle High German wir, the first-person plural nominative pronoun across Germanic languages.
wir.notes: Its accusative and dative form uns shares its root with English 'us'.

wissen.etymology: Continues Old High German wizzan and Middle High German wizzen, an ancient preterite-present literally meaning 'to have seen' and therefore 'to know as a fact'.

wollen.etymology: Goes back to Old High German wellen and Middle High German wellen / wollen ('to wish, choose, intend'), sharing an ancient optative heritage with Latin velle and English 'will'.

zedernkiste.etymology: Compound of Zeder ('cedar', OHG zēdarboum from Latin cedrus / Greek kédros) + Kiste ('box, chest', OHG kista from Latin cista); see DWDS/Pfeifer under Zeder and Kiste.

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Kiste
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Kiste

zehnte.etymology: Pfeifer (DWDS) and Kluge trace zehnte through OHG zehanto and MHG zehende, the inherited Indo-European ordinal of zehn (cognate with English tenth and Latin decimus).

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): zehnte
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): zehnte

zeichnen.etymology: Pfeifer (DWDS) and Kluge derive zeichnen (OHG zeihhanen, MHG zeichenen 'to mark with a sign, delineate') from Zeichen ('sign, mark', cognate with English token).

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): zeichnen
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): zeichnen

ziegelhaus.etymology: Compound of der Ziegel ('brick, tile', an early Roman building loan from Latin tēgula) + das Haus ('house'), naming a traditional brick house.

zimmer.etymology: Old High German zimbar and Middle High German zimber originally meant 'building timber' (cognate with English 'timber'), then 'wooden structure', and finally an individual 'room'.

zitrone.etymology: Borrowed in the 16th century from Italian citrone, derived from Latin citrus ('citron tree').

zitronenkuchen.etymology: Compound of die Zitrone ('lemon', via Italian citrone from Latin citrus) + linking -n- + der Kuchen ('cake', OHG kuocho). Although Zitrone is feminine, the final element Kuchen makes der Zitronenkuchen masculine.

zitronentörtchen.etymology: Compound of Zitrone ('lemon', 16th c. from Italian citrone) + Törtchen (diminutive in -chen of Torte 'tart, layer cake', from Italian torta); see DWDS/Pfeifer under Zitrone and Törtchen.

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): Törtchen
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): Törtchen

zu.etymology: Recorded in Old High German in stressed form zuo and unstressed zi / za, and in Middle High German as zuo / ze. Modern zu serves as dative preposition ('to'), infinitive marker, degree adverb ('too'), and predicative/separable 'shut'.
zu.notes: Contracts with dem to zum and with der to zur.

zug.etymology: Old High German zug and Middle High German zuc ('act of pulling, procession, draft'), a verbal noun from ziehen ('to pull'). With the arrival of railways in the 19th century, a string of pulled carriages became Eisenbahnzug and simply der Zug.

zum.etymology: Standard contraction of the preposition zu ('to') with the masculine or neuter dative singular article dem (Middle High German zem / zum).

zumachen.etymology: Separable compound of stressed zu ('shut, closed') + machen ('make'), serving in everyday speech alongside schließen ('to close').

zur.etymology: Standard contraction of the preposition zu ('to') with the feminine dative singular article der (Middle High German zer / zur).

zusammenbringen.etymology: Separable compound of zusammen ('together', OHG zisamane) + mixed verb bringen ('to bring', OHG bringan); documented in DWDS/Pfeifer under zusammenbringen.

sources.title: DWDS / Pfeifer (Etymologisches Wörterbuch des Deutschen): zusammenbringen
Kluge, Etymologisches Wörterbuch der deutschen Sprache (25. Aufl.): zusammenbringen

öffnen.etymology: Derived from the adjective offen ('open') via Old High German offanōn and Middle High German offenen / öffnen ('to make open').
